source.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly measures training and test accuracy after iterative pruning, comparing the gap between winning-ticket subnetworks and their dense parent networks. This is a conceptual test of generalization behavior, although its central intervention is finding sparse subnetworks rather than the claim versions' specified random-label, width, optimizer-comparison, batch-size, or sharpness experiments.
record.gate_note: Reports training and test accuracy for pruned winning tickets, dense parent networks, and randomly reinitialized tickets. Cited claims from prior work are not extracted as results. Figure-only curves are not assigned reconstructed values; text-reported aggregate results are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study tests V6 through dropout versus no-dropout held-out accuracy comparisons, including unpruned networks, and V4 through explicit Adam versus SGD validation-accuracy comparisons. These results are missing from the extracted rows. Pruning and initialization results alone do not test any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct: pruning uncovers sparse subnetworks whose original initializations enable comparable training time and parent-level or better test accuracy, often with smaller training-test gaps. Ticket discovery depends on learning rate and warmup in deeper networks, and evidence is restricted to MNIST and CIFAR10. The proposed explanation that SGD seeks out these subnetworks remains an untested conjecture.
record.recipe_differences: Iterative or one-shot magnitude pruning of dense networks followed by resetting surviving weights to their original initialization; this differs from all eight versioned experiments. Results use MNIST and CIFAR10 vision classifiers. The study varies optimizers, dropout, learning rates, warmup, and pruning, but does not test the corresponding version claims as specified.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate and warmup strongly affect whether tickets are found in deeper VGG-19 and Resnet-18; pruning strategy and rate affect ticket size and performance; dropout changes test accuracy and learning-speed patterns; pruning convolutional versus fully connected layers changes results.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-informed magnitude pruning with original initializations can preserve or improve test accuracy and reduce training-test gaps; success depends on sparsity, architecture, learning rate, and warmup.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dense MNIST and CIFAR10 classifiers contain sparse subnetworks that can match or exceed parent accuracy when trained from their original initializations.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing Gaussian noise in ticket initializations reduces subsequent accuracy and slows learning, while moderate perturbations retain advantages over random reinitialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Winning-ticket training performance depends on initialization but tolerates some initialization noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Resampling ticket initialization distributions does not recover ticket performance, and pruning at initialization performs worse than training-informed selection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ticket performance depends on the arrangement and training-informed selection of initial weights beyond their marginal distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Eventual ticket weights move farther during dense-network training than other weights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Winning-ticket membership is associated with larger initial-to-final weight displacement.

record.problems: Experiments cover only MNIST and CIFAR10, not larger datasets; the authors note iterative pruning is computationally intensive. Many reported curves are figures, with several exact values unavailable in the text. Training and test gap comparisons are partly conveyed through accuracy trends and the statement that training accuracy reaches 100%, rather than a tabulated gap metric.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out for the 17 reported text-based outcomes retained. Numerous plotted hyperparameter sweeps in Appendices G–I are not separately extracted because their per-condition values are figure-only and the text summarizes only selected trends; see Figures 26–45. Figure 1 random sparse network comparisons are not extracted as exact result rows because the text gives only the qualitative trend and the figure is plotted.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label training and held-out comparison.

No width sweep establishing continued test-error reduction beyond the width required for zero training error. Appendix G.6 studies two-hidden-layer networks and selected sparse tickets without establishing this threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison on the same image task, or test of learning local connectivity.
No language benchmarks, broader optimizer tuning, decoupled weight decay, or Adam-to-SGD switching. The reported optimizer comparisons do not establish matched training performance.

No very-small-training-set comparison, dropout-rate sweep establishing underfitting, or removal of dropout and weight decay together with augmentation. Dropout comparisons also change learning rates and available training iterations.
No trained-network magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or ranking against competing generalization measures.
Removes weights rather than training examples; no memorization-based example selection.

missing.what: Separate unpruned dropout comparisons: test accuracy increases by 2.1 points for Conv-2, 3.0 for Conv-4, and 2.4 for Conv-6. Record dropout rate 0.5, changed learning rates, threefold training allowance, and accuracy evaluated at minimum validation loss.
missing.locator: Section 3, Dropout; Figure 6; Appendices H.1 and H.5

missing.what: Explicit optimizer comparison: unpruned SGD-trained convolutional networks typically achieve 2–3 points lower validation accuracy than Adam at best; higher SGD rates cause exploding gradients and lower rates often fail to learn. This textual comparison is distinct from the declared omission of individual sweep values.

Explicit comparison of pruned Lenet: SGD rates 0.4/0.8 achieve validation accuracy equivalent to the best Adam rates 0.0012/0.002. Record this separately from learning-speed and attainable-sparsity comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The reader incorrectly excludes the explicit dropout and optimizer comparisons. All 17 existing rows concern other findings, so their states are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; this does not invalidate their pruning results. The dropout accuracy gains support the configured training recipe, while changed learning rates and training allowance prevent isolating dropout's contribution.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.
No one-hidden-layer width sweep beyond interpolation is tested.
No controlled convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison of generalization is tested.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD for held-out performance is tested.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison is tested.
Dropout is evaluated in combination with pruning; the study does not test whether dropout itself lowers test error against an otherwise matched no-dropout model as stated in the version.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and competing generalization measures are not tested.
No memorized-example removal experiment is tested.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100)
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with surviving weights reset to their original initialization; test and training accuracy compared with dense parent.
rows.measure: Test accuracy at iteration 50,000; training accuracy reaches 100% for nearly all networks.
rows.baseline: Original dense network test accuracy; exact value not stated in text.
rows.value: Test accuracy improves by up to 0.35 percentage points; training accuracy reaches 100% for nearly all networks.
rows.note: Authors state that the gap between training and test accuracy is smaller for winning tickets. Exact plotted values are not given in text.
rows.check: Pruning does not test a listed version. The 13.5% sparsity accompanies the early-stopping improvement; the text does not explicitly assign the maximum 0.35-point final-training improvement to that sparsity.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), randomly reinitialized winning ticket
rows.operation_detail: Retain winning-ticket mask but randomly reinitialize surviving weights; compare with original-initialization tickets.
rows.baseline: Original-initialization winning ticket at the same sparsity; exact accuracy not stated.
rows.value: Test accuracy is half a percentage point lower than the winning ticket; networks at Pm ≥ 5% reach 100% training accuracy.
rows.note: Comparison concerns the importance of initialization and generalization; no random-label condition.
rows.check: Initialization comparison, not a listed version. The half-point accuracy difference is reported at early stopping, not explicitly at iteration 50,000. Duplicates the accuracy comparison in R13.

rows.subject: Conv-2
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with original initialization retained; compare test and training accuracy with dense parent.

conditions.value: Pm ≥ 2%; best test-accuracy improvement at Pm = 4.6%

rows.baseline: Original dense Conv-2 test accuracy; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Best test accuracy improves by 3.4 percentage points; training accuracy reaches 100% for all networks when Pm ≥ 2%.
rows.note: The paper says the training-test gap is smaller for winning tickets.
rows.check: Pruning does not test a listed version. The 3.4-point improvement at 4.6% remaining is an early-stopping result; final-training accuracy is separately described as higher without a numerical improvement.

rows.subject: Conv-4
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with original initialization retained; compare test and training accuracy with dense parent.

conditions.value: Pm ≥ 2%; best test-accuracy improvement at Pm = 11.1%

rows.baseline: Original dense Conv-4 test accuracy; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Best test accuracy improves by 3.5 percentage points; training accuracy reaches 100% for all networks when Pm ≥ 2%.
rows.note: The paper says the training-test gap is smaller for winning tickets.
rows.check: Pruning does not test a listed version. The 3.5-point improvement at 11.1% remaining is an early-stopping result, not a stated improvement at iteration 25,000.

rows.subject: Conv-6
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with original initialization retained; compare test and training accuracy with dense parent.

conditions.value: Pm ≥ 2%; best test-accuracy improvement at Pm = 26.4%

rows.baseline: Original dense Conv-6 test accuracy; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Best test accuracy improves by 3.3 percentage points; training accuracy reaches 100% for all networks when Pm ≥ 2%.
rows.note: The paper says the training-test gap is smaller for winning tickets.
rows.check: Pruning does not test a listed version. The 3.3-point improvement at 26.4% remaining is an early-stopping result, not a stated improvement at iteration 30,000.

rows.subject: VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with global pruning and original initialization retained.
rows.measure: Test accuracy at 30K, 60K, and 112K iterations relative to original and randomly reinitialized subnetworks.
rows.baseline: Original network and randomly reinitialized subnetworks; exact values not stated.
rows.value: At learning rate 0.1, iterative pruning does not find winning tickets; performance is no better than random reinitialization.
rows.locator: Section 4; Figure 7; Appendix I.1, Figures 38 and 40
rows.note: No exact plotted values recovered. Authors report that warmup enables winning tickets at the higher learning rate.
rows.check: Measures whether pruning finds winning tickets, not any listed effect.

rows.subject: VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with global pruning and original initialization retained.
rows.measure: Test accuracy at 30K, 60K, and 112K iterations relative to original network.
rows.baseline: Original dense network test accuracy; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Subnetworks remain within 1 percentage point of original accuracy when Pm ≥ 3.5%; they do not match the original accuracy.
rows.note: The text explicitly says these are not winning tickets because they do not match original accuracy.
rows.check: Measures sparse-network accuracy retention, not any listed effect.

rows.subject: VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with learning-rate warmup and original initialization retained.
rows.measure: Test accuracy relative to unpruned network.
rows.baseline: Unpruned network test accuracy; warmup improves it by about one percentage point over the non-warmup unpruned network.
rows.value: Warmup makes it possible to find winning tickets, exceeding the initial accuracy when Pm ≥ 1.5%.
rows.note: Result is about sparse-ticket performance and training setup, not any listed claim version.
rows.check: Warmup is tested for finding winning tickets without a batch-size comparison; this does not test V5.

rows.subject: Resnet-18
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with global pruning and original initialization retained.
rows.measure: Test accuracy at 10K, 20K, and 30K iterations relative to original and randomly reinitialized subnetworks.
rows.baseline: Original network and randomly reinitialized subnetworks; exact values not stated.
rows.value: At learning rate 0.1, iterative pruning does not find winning tickets.
rows.check: Measures whether pruning finds winning tickets, not any listed effect.

rows.subject: Resnet-18
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with global pruning and original initialization retained.
rows.baseline: Original network at higher learning rate 0.1: 90.5% test accuracy.
rows.value: Best winning-ticket accuracy at the lower learning rate is 89.5%.
rows.note: Winning tickets at the lower learning rate fall short of the original network's accuracy at the higher learning rate.
rows.check: The 89.5% versus 90.5% comparison changes learning rate as well as sparsity. Tickets at the lower learning rate satisfy the authors' ticket criterion against their corresponding parent; the cross-rate deficit does not establish partial satisfaction of a listed version.

rows.subject: Resnet-18
rows.operation_detail: Iterative magnitude pruning with learning-rate warmup and original initialization retained.
rows.baseline: Original network at learning rate 0.1: 90.5% test accuracy.
rows.locator: Section 4; Figure 8; Appendix I.1, Figures 39 and 44
rows.note: Authors report no tested warmup hyperparameters could identify winning tickets at learning rate 0.1.
rows.check: Sparse-network accuracy with warmup does not test a listed version; no batch-size comparison is made.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), one-shot winning ticket
rows.operation_detail: One-shot magnitude pruning, then reset surviving weights to original initialization.
rows.measure: Test accuracy and early-stopping iteration relative to dense parent.
rows.baseline: Original dense network; exact test accuracy and iteration not stated.
rows.value: Test accuracy is higher than original when 95.0% ≥ Pm ≥ 5.17%; early-stopping is earlier when 67.5% ≥ Pm ≥ 17.6%.
rows.note: One-shot pruning results are text-reported as ranges.
rows.check: One-shot pruning and learning speed do not test any listed version.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), randomly reinitialized winning ticket
rows.operation_detail: Random reinitialization of the mask selected by iterative pruning.
rows.measure: Minimum validation loss time and test accuracy.
rows.baseline: Original-initialization ticket at Pm = 21%; exact baseline test accuracy not stated.
rows.value: Minimum validation loss occurs 2.51x later than for the winning ticket; test accuracy is half a percentage point lower.
rows.note: Authors state all networks reach 100% training accuracy for Pm ≥ 5%.
rows.check: Initialization comparison, not a listed version. Merge its duplicated accuracy comparison with R2 while retaining the additional early-stopping-time result.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), winning-ticket weights with Gaussian noise
rows.operation_detail: Add Gaussian noise to winning-ticket initializations, with layer noise standard deviation a multiple of initialization standard deviation.
rows.baseline: Unperturbed winning ticket; exact values not stated.
rows.value: Noise reduces test accuracy and slows learning as noise increases; 0.5σ barely changes accuracy; 3σ tickets still outperform random reinitialization.
rows.note: Text summarizes the trend; individual point values are figure-only.
rows.check: Perturbs initialization before retraining and measures subsequent performance; it does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness of trained networks or its correlation with generalization gaps.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), winning-ticket weights with initialization sampled from ticket distribution
rows.operation_detail: Randomly resample ticket weights from the per-layer distribution of initializations present in the winning ticket.
rows.baseline: Original winning-ticket initialization and reinitialization from the original Gaussian distribution; exact values not stated.
rows.value: Sampled-ticket initializations perform little better than random reinitialization from the original distribution.
rows.note: The authors also report similar results for SGD-trained tickets.
rows.check: Resampling initial weights does not test any listed version.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), tickets pruned at iteration 0
rows.operation_detail: Magnitude-prune before any training, then train the sparse network with Adam.
rows.baseline: Iterative pruning with training-informed ticket selection; exact values not stated.
rows.value: These networks perform even worse than iteratively pruned and randomly reinitialized tickets.
rows.note: This tests a different pruning procedure; exact plotted values are not given.
rows.check: Compares pruning procedures, not a listed effect; worse performance under a different procedure is not a reversal of any listed claim.

rows.subject: Lenet (Lenet-300-100), weights in eventual winning tickets
rows.operation_detail: Compare the magnitude of weight changes from initial to final values for weights in and outside the eventual ticket.
rows.measure: Distribution of absolute final-minus-initial weight changes.
rows.baseline: Weights not in eventual winning ticket; exact distribution values not stated.
rows.value: Winning-ticket weights tend to change by a larger amount than weights outside the ticket.
rows.note: Authors say this does not support the hypothesis that ticket weights were already close to the optimum.
rows.check: Weight displacement is not a generalization comparison or a magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
